name: Stem Separation and Restoration
title: Stem Separation and Restoration
answer: Stem separation and restoration covers the work of pulling a finished recording apart into its component parts, typically vocals, drums, bass and a residual instrumental, and of repairing damage in old or badly captured audio. It sits alongside mixing and mastering in the music production chain, and it is also used in archival work, sampling, karaoke and remix production. Restoration is the mirror task: removing noise, clicks, hum and clipping rather than isolating instruments. Both are treated here as one family because they share the same underlying models and the same listening tests.

sections.body: Stem separation and restoration covers the work of pulling a finished recording apart into its component parts, typically vocals, drums, bass and a residual instrumental, and of repairing damage in old or badly captured audio. It sits alongside mixing and mastering in the music production chain, and it is also used in archival work, sampling, karaoke and remix production. Restoration is the mirror task: removing noise, clicks, hum and clipping rather than isolating instruments. Both are treated here as one family because they share the same underlying models and the same listening tests.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on source separation models, most of which are trained on large collections of mixed and isolated recordings, and on spectral processing for the restoration side. Practitioners usually work in a digital audio workstation with a separation plugin or a standalone tool, and heavier jobs run on a GPU either locally or rented by the hour. Output is delivered as separate audio files, often as WAV or lossless stems, and sometimes as MIDI or notation when the goal is transcription rather than remixing. The site tracks 2000 audio models, and separation and restoration account for a visible share of that catalogue.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical job starts with a clean, high resolution copy of the source, since artefacts in the input are amplified in the output. The engineer runs a separation model, listens to each stem against the original, and then cleans up bleed, smearing and metallic artefacts with EQ, gating and spectral repair. Restoration follows a similar loop: identify the defect, apply a targeted process, and compare before and after on both speakers and headphones. The final check is always a listening test, because separation metrics do not reliably predict what a mix engineer will hear.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights are the hard part. Separating a commercial recording does not create a new right in the underlying composition or the master, and releasing stems or a remix normally requires clearance from both the publisher and the rights holder of the recording. Restoration of archival material raises its own questions about who owns the restored file and whether the restoration is protected in its own right. The site currently tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, and several of those turn on training data and output ownership. Provenance matters too: keeping a record of which model, version and settings produced a stem is now standard practice in professional workflows.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Quality keeps improving, particularly on difficult material such as dense mixes, live recordings and heavily compressed masters, and the gap between dedicated tools and general purpose audio models is narrowing. Restoration is moving toward end to end systems that handle several defects at once rather than one process per problem. The open questions are less technical than commercial and legal: how stems are licensed, how training data is accounted for, and whether restored archival recordings attract their own protection. Expect the tooling to become more embedded in the DAW and less of a separate step.
